evidence_quotes.quote: The case of a joint water supply project between the Mautu rural community and the Cameroon Development Corporation (CDC) is explored to examine an emerging paradigm of partnership by communities in rural Cameroon to foster access to piped domestic water supply.

During the last phase of data collection, 25 semi-structured interviews, and one town hall meeting were conducted to gather information on the operation and maintenance of the system, and the problems and the solution perceptions.

The management committee in collaboration with the village council established rules and regulations regarding the operation of the taps and activities near the water source.  To generate income to carry out minor repairs and maintenance (repair/replacement of damaged pipes and taps) by a care-taker, having a basic plumbing knowledge, private connections were charged a one time connection fee (5000CFA, approximately $10 USD).
As standpipe water is supplied for free and private connections are only charged a connection fee, funds for repairs and maintenance are levied irregularly as needed.
This is attributed to CDC negotiating only with the chief and not also with the village council and their advisors to decide on the terms of the agreement for joint exploitation of the water source.
At the time of the meetings three of the six public standpipes had no taps, and one damaged standpipe had remained closed for a long time.

Due to these problems, children were arriving late to school (after their water fetching duties) and many households had reverted to the use of unprotected springs considered as unsafe compared to the spring that was harnessed for the project (also the flow of several other springs had reduced or dried up).

criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural community and household access to piped domestic water supply via public standpipes and private yard/house connections in Mautu village, Cameroon.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines institutional, governance, and regulatory factors in a joint parastatal-community water supply project. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, while parts of the paper discuss project planning and capacity building, it directly analyses rule-type mechanisms governing service access: (1) the institutional/contractual partnership and resource-sharing terms negotiated solely between the parastatal Cameroon Development Corporation (CDC) and the traditional Chief (allocating 96% of flow to CDC and 4% to Mautu without renegotiation provisions or state regulatory oversight of corporate-community water partnerships); (2) community tariff and cost-recovery rules (free water provision at standpipes and private taps, a one-time 5,000 CFA private connection fee, and irregular ad-hoc repair levies with non-payment); and (3) absence of administrative regulation or inspection of private household connections despite fee collection.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical qualitative case study collecting primary data in three phases: 5 key informant interviews, physical inspection of the water network, 25 semi-structured interviews, opportunistic interviews, and 2 town-hall meetings with 176 participants. Per review rules, qualitative empirical socio-legal/governance studies are eligible regardless of lack of quantitative effect sizes.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete service access, reliability, availability, and exclusion/reversion outcomes: severe low water pressure at peak demand, long waiting times, lack of standpipes in new residential areas, breakdown/closure of public standpipes (3 of 6 missing taps and 1 closed long-term), >30% household private connection uptake, and household reversion to unsafe unprotected springs.
criterion_notes.c5: Population (Mautu rural community and households in Cameroon, with sample sizes reported for interviews and town-hall meetings), exposure (joint parastatal-community agreement structure, local tariff/cost-recovery rules, and unregulated private connection rules), outcome (standpipe availability/functionality, peak-hour water pressure, waiting times, and reversion to unprotected springs), and study design (three-phase qualitative case study) are all clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

study_design: Qualitative empirical case study (key informant and semi-structured interviews, public town-hall meetings, and physical system inspection)
population_and_sample: Rural community and households of Mautu village, South West Region, Cameroon (population over 4,000; sample comprising 5 key informant interviews, 25 semi-structured interviews, opportunistic interviews, physical network inspection, and 2 town-hall meetings with 176 participants).
exposure: Joint parastatal-community water supply partnership terms and local governance/tariff rules: bilateral agreement between Cameroon Development Corporation (CDC) and traditional Chief without Village Council consultation or regulatory oversight (allocating 96% vs. 4% of spring flow), free water policy with one-time 5,000 CFA private connection fee and irregular repair levies, and uninspected household connections.
outcome: Piped domestic water availability, peak-hour water pressure and reliability, waiting times, standpipe functionality (3 of 6 standpipes without taps and 1 closed), coverage in new neighborhoods, private household connection uptake (>30%), and household reversion to unprotected springs.
rationale: This empirical qualitative case study from rural Cameroon meets all inclusion criteria (c1-c6). It investigates community and household piped water access in Mautu village and links concrete access and reliability outcomes (peak-hour low pressure, non-functional standpipes, lack of network expansion, and reversion to unprotected springs) to rule-type governance and cost-recovery mechanisms: an unregulated joint supply agreement negotiated solely between a parastatal corporation (CDC) and the village Chief that allocated only 4% of spring flow to the community, local cost-recovery rules providing water free of charge alongside a one-time 5,000 CFA connection fee and ad-hoc repair levies, and uninspected private connections. Confidence is medium because the study combines rule-type contractual, tariff, and connection-regulation mechanisms with broader project planning and O&M capacity issues.
